passage: Ayesha, come here. I'm Elizabeth. I was ten when my father lost his job. He sat us down and said, "My work has stopped. I will look for another one. We are okay, and we will not lose our home right now." I went quiet. Then I asked, "Will I still get my school shoes?" He laughed a bit, and said, "Yes, you will." After that I went outside and played gilli-danda till dark, as if nothing was different. That night I woke up and cried and could not say why. My mother sat by the bed and held my hand. I was glad they told me plainly. Not knowing would have been worse.

qa.q: How old was Elizabeth when Elizabeth's father lost his job?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling that night when waking and crying?
qa.a: A delayed sadness and fear that had not shown during the day, though Elizabeth could not say why.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's father do that reassured Elizabeth?
qa.a: He told the children plainly that his work had stopped, that he would look for another job, and that the family was okay for now.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother have seen Elizabeth's reaction that night?
qa.a: With care. The mother sat by the bed and held Elizabeth's hand without needing an explanation for the tears.

grounding: A child told about the father's job loss goes quiet, asks an odd question, keeps playing, and cries later; a plain honest explanation helps.

passage: The rain was heavy and the school bus was due in ten minutes. Noor knelt by Joseph's chair. "Joseph, I have sad news. Bruno died in the night. He was old and he wasn't in pain." Joseph looked at the cereal bowl. "Will he be cold?" Noor swallowed. "No, sweetheart. He is not feeling cold or anything now." Joseph nodded, finished the cereal, put on the raincoat, and asked, "Can I take my umbrella with the duck?" Noor stared, then said, "Of course." At bedtime that night, Joseph crept into the room and said, "I miss Bruno." Noor held Joseph close, and they cried together.

qa.q: What did Joseph ask Noor after hearing the news?
qa.a: "Will he be cold?"

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when asking for the umbrella with the duck?
qa.a: Probably taking the news in slowly, carrying on with everyday things while the sadness had not yet arrived.

qa.q: What did Noor do that helped Joseph?
qa.a: Noor told the news simply and honestly, answered the odd question calmly, and later held Joseph close at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt seeing Joseph ask about the umbrella?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps unsure, but Noor stayed calm and said "Of course," accepting that children react in different ways.

grounding: A child told a pet has died goes quiet, asks odd questions and carries on, with the sadness arriving later, even under a time constraint.

passage:
"Raghav, Papa has something to tell you," said Mummy.
Papa sat down. "I lost my job today, beta. The company closed."
Raghav stared at him. Then he asked, "Will we still have Bruno?"
"Yes. Bruno stays."
"And my cycle?"
"Your cycle stays too."
"Okay." Raghav went back to his building blocks.
Later that night, his older brother Divyansh found him awake. "You okay?"
"I don't know. Are we going to be poor?"
"Papa's looking for a new job. It might be tight for a while. But we're okay."
Raghav was quiet. Then he started crying. "I was scared to ask Papa."
Divyansh sat on the bed. "You can ask him anything. He told us because he trusts us."

qa.q: What did Raghav ask about first after the news?
qa.a: He asked, 'Will we still have Bruno?'

qa.q: Why did Raghav carry on playing and cry later?
qa.a: He was scared and unsure, and his feelings came out later, when he was alone with Divyansh.

qa.q: How did Divyansh help Raghav?
qa.a: He listened, gave a simple honest answer, and reassured Raghav he could ask Papa anything.

qa.q: How might Papa feel knowing Raghav was scared to ask?
qa.a: Papa would probably feel sad and want to reassure him more openly.

grounding: Shows a child hearing about a parent's job loss, asking odd questions and playing on, with the real reaction arriving later.

passage:
When Kavitha didi told me our cat Mishti had died, I said, "Oh," and went back to my puzzle. Didi looked worried. She said, "Are you okay?" I said, "Yes. Can I finish my puzzle?"
I didn't cry that day. I even asked if Mishti could still eat her food in heaven, which made didi laugh and cry at the same time.
Three days later, I saw Mishti's blue bowl in the kitchen, and I just started crying and couldn't stop. Didi held me. She said it was normal to feel sad later, not right away.
She told me the truth about how Mishti died. Simply. That she was very old and her heart stopped. I think that helped more than if she'd said Mishti went away.
I'm Hafsa, and I still keep the blue bowl.

qa.q: What colour was Mishti's bowl?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when seeing the bowl three days later?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a wave of sadness and grief, crying and unable to stop.

qa.q: What did Kavitha didi do that helped Hafsa?
qa.a: She explained simply and honestly how Mishti died, and said it was normal to feel sad later, not right away.

qa.q: How did Kavitha didi feel when Hafsa went back to the puzzle?
qa.a: She looked worried, unsure if Hafsa was okay.

grounding: Shows a child hearing of a pet's death with a delayed reaction, and honest, simple explanation reassuring more than hiding.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday.
Lalit (8) was unusually quiet today. At lunch he asked Dilnaz, his deskmate, "Do you think a car can be sold for a lot of money?" Later he asked me, "If a dad stops working, does he stay home forever?"
I asked if something had happened. He said, "Papa doesn't go to the office anymore. The office said no." Then he went back to his drawing as if nothing was wrong.
I didn't press. I told him, "Thank you for telling me. It's okay to have questions." I called his mother after school. She confirmed that his father had lost his job last week and they had told the children briefly. I suggested a short, honest talk at home, and I'll keep an eye on him this week.

qa.q: Who is Lalit's deskmate?
qa.a: Dilnaz.

qa.q: What do Lalit's questions suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he was worried and confused about his father's job loss, even though he carried on drawing.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next that could help Lalit?
qa.a: They thanked him, called his mother, suggested a short honest talk at home, and planned to watch him this week.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Lalit asked about selling a car?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably puzzled, not knowing why he asked.

grounding: Shows a child told of a parent's job loss reacting quietly with odd questions, and adults responding with honest simple explanation.

passage:
Friday
Wasim's diary. Mummy and Papa called me to the sofa after dinner. Papa said his office has closed and he doesn't have a job now. Mummy said we will be okay, we have enough for now, Papa will look for a new job, and none of it is my fault. I said "okay" and then I asked if the office chairs will be thrown away. I don't know why I asked that. Then I went down and played cricket with Kavitha for a long time and didn't tell her anything.
Now it's late and my stomach feels funny. Will we still go to Nana's in May? I'll ask Mummy tomorrow. She said I can ask anything, even strange things. She said the chair question was fine.

qa.q: What did Wasim ask after hearing the news?
qa.a: Wasim asked if the office chairs will be thrown away.

qa.q: How is Wasim feeling late that night?
qa.a: Wasim feels uneasy and a bit worried, with a funny stomach and a question about going to Nana's in May.

qa.q: What did Mummy and Papa do that helped?
qa.a: They explained simply and honestly, said it wasn't Wasim's fault, and said Wasim could ask anything, even strange things.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have seen Wasim that evening?
qa.a: She probably saw a friend playing cricket as usual, with no idea of the news Wasim was carrying.

grounding: Shows a child reacting to a parent's job loss with an odd question and ordinary play, reassured by an honest, simple explanation.
